vignette: Sarojini, an 80-year-old South Asian woman with a warm and engaging presence, has dedicated her life to dentistry. Over the years, she has seen countless patients and provided them with quality care, but it was a terrorist attack at one of her clinics that left indelible marks on her psyche. Sarojini is divorced and lives alone, maintaining an active lifestyle despite her age. The day of the incident was like any other until it wasn’t. It began as a busy clinic morning in 2015 when she received word over the intercom that a patient had arrived for their scheduled appointment. The door opened to reveal not just one patient but several masked individuals wielding weapons. Sarojini, along with her staff and patients, were held hostage for hours while the terrorists demanded ransom and made threatening demands. Since then, Sarojini has struggled with vivid flashbacks that often transport her back to those harrowing moments. She can still hear the gunshots ringing in her ears and feel the terror of not knowing if she would make it out alive. These intrusive memories are triggered by loud noises, even something as mundane as a door slamming or the sound of sirens passing by on the street. Sarojini’s daily routine has been significantly affected. She avoids crowded places, which means her visits to the local market or community center have dwindled considerably. The fear of encountering something that might trigger a flashback keeps her indoors more often than not. Even watching news programs can be overwhelming as she worries about hearing reports of another terrorist attack. In her dental clinic, Sarojini has implemented new security measures and hired additional staff to ensure the safety of everyone involved. She meticulously plans each day to avoid any situations that might provoke distressing memories. While she still practices dentistry part-time, she often finds herself feeling on edge during appointments, scanning the room for signs of potential danger. Sarojini’s sleep has been severely disrupted since the attack. Nightmares punctuate her nights, and upon waking, she often feels disoriented and overwhelmed by a sense of dread. The dreams are so vivid that they feel like reliving the trauma all over again. She frequently checks locks on windows and doors multiple times before falling asleep, sometimes even staying awake to avoid the torment. Her relationship with her ex-husband has been strained since the attack as well. They had remained cordial over the years but now find it difficult to connect without discussing the incident or inadvertently triggering each other’s anxieties. Sarojini often feels a profound sense of guilt for not being able to protect herself and those around her, which exacerbates feelings of helplessness. Despite these challenges, Sarojini remains resilient in her profession. Her deep-rooted dedication to dentistry has provided her with a sense of purpose during difficult times. She finds solace in the structure and routine that her work provides, even though it is no longer as fulfilling as it once was. Colleagues and patients have noticed changes in her demeanor but respect her need for caution. Sarojini’s life is now a delicate balance between managing her trauma symptoms and maintaining her sense of self. While she has not sought formal treatment yet, she acknowledges the toll this experience has taken on her mental health. Her story underscores how deeply an act of terrorism can impact one's life long after the event itself.
